newsitem.title: USA: Cuban exile flotilla protests drownings off Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Cuban exile flotilla protests drownings off Cuba.

text.p: Cuban exiles sailed across the Florida Straits on Sunday in a protest flotilla to mark the anniversary of the death of 41 people who drowned while fleeing Cuba in 1994.
Cuban naval gunboats watched the protest from a distance, but did not intervene, and the flotilla of 15 boats sailed back to Florida without incident, organisers said.
The U.S. Coast Guard seized the flotilla's lead boat at the outset because its leader had vowed to enter Cuban territorial waters, a Coast Guard spokeswoman said.
"We seized the vessel 'Democracia'," spokeswoman Petty Officer Veronica Bandrowsky said. "(It) was the only vessel that stated that it had intention to enter Cuban territorial seas."
The Coast Guard allowed the flotilla to sail south where the boats, accompanied by several planes, stopped about 12 miles (19 km) off Cuba's coast for a memorial service.

Ramon Saul Sanchez, the head of the Cuban exile group Democracy Movement whose boat was stopped by the Coast Guard, said participants had radioed back that their brief service was watched but not approached by three Cuban gunboats.
"They remained probably four miles into Cuban waters, probably alert to what we were doing, but they didn't do anything in any certain way," he told Reuters.

Sanchez was not arrested, but he said he disagreed with the U.S. action in preventing his protest against Cuba's communist regime and was thinking of suing the U.S. government on the grounds that the seizure was unconstitutional.

"The fact that the United States takes the same position as the Cuban government in denying our rights ... to peacefully return to our country goes against the best traditions of this nation in terms of civil rights," he said.

The lastest waterborne protest by Cuban exiles marked the anniversary of the drowning of 41 people who were attempting to leave Cuba aboard a stolen boat that sank on July 13, 1994, after it was rammed by a Cuban naval vessel.

The U.S. government had warned flotilla participants to respect Cuba's territory and urged Cuba's government to act prudently toward the flotilla. The Cuban government regards the flotillas as provocations.
Coast Guard vessels were in the Florida Straits to keep track of the flotilla boats as they proceeded.
In February 1996 Cuban MiG fighters shot down two small planes piloted by members of Brothers to the Rescue near the island, killing the four Cuban-American fliers and sparking a diplomatic crisis.
Members of the exile group Brothers to the Rescue joined the flotilla on Sunday by flying over the protest memorial.

There was no immediate indication of a link between Miami's Cuban exile community and the bombing of two Havana tourist hotels on Saturday. The Cuban government said it had evidence "people" from the United States were responsible.
Three people were hurt in the blasts that damaged the lobbies of two landmark hotels.
Leading exile groups in Miami, including Sanchez's Democracy Movement, denied any link to the blasts, which they said arose from the supression of democratic rights in Cuba.
